blocks.content: The Central Vigilance Commission is mainly an advisory body and has no power to register criminal cases or directly sanction prosecution.

rows: Supervisory and advisory body on vigilance administration
Primary investigative agency for corruption and complex crimes
Statutory body created under CVC Act, 2003
Non-statutory body deriving investigative powers from DSPE Act, 1946
Cannot register criminal FIRs or conduct direct arrests
Empowered to register FIRs, conduct searches, and arrest accused
Charge-sheets submitted directly to special courts

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The Central Vigilance Commission is primarily an advisory body, meaning its recommendations are not legally binding on central government ministries or departments.
CVC lacks its own dedicated investigative machinery and relies largely on the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) or departmental chief vigilance officers.
It cannot directly register criminal cases or prosecute offenders independently without sanction from the competent authority.
The powers of CVC are restricted to central government employees and specified public sector undertakings, excluding state personnel and private entities.
If the executive authority disagrees with the advice of CVC, it must record reasons in writing and communicate them to the Commission.
CVC advice is strictly advisory; non-acceptance of CVC advice by ministries must be reported to the CVC and incorporated into its annual report presented to Parliament.
CVC derives statutory status from the CVC Act of 2003, based on the initial recommendations of the Santhanam Committee (1962–64).
CVC exercises superintendence over the functioning of CBI only in matters relating to the investigation of offenses under the Prevention of Corruption Act.
